audience: Beginners to spec-driven and agentic coding workflows
lead_scenario: You've joined the engineering team at a startup building ContextCafe - the web app for a cozy neighborhood coffee shop, where regulars browse the seasonal menu, place mobile orders, and earn loyalty rewards. The team is retiring its ad-hoc vibe coding habits and adopting spec-driven development with an agentic coding assistant.

skills.skill: Distinguishing vibe coding from spec-driven development
behaviors: Identify the characteristics and limitations of vibe coding
Explain the core benefits of specs: controlling large changes with small edits, reducing context decay, and improving intent fidelity

skills.skill: Understanding the SDD workflow and the developer's role
behaviors: Describe the cycle of constitution, feature loops, and replanning
Recognize the human's role as architect and supervisor who supplies context
Select the right level of detail to give an agent
Identify the three constitution pillars: mission, tech stack, and roadmap
Draft the constitution through human-in-the-loop conversation with the agent
Maintain the constitution as a living, version-controlled document
Plan a feature spec covering plan, requirements, and validation before coding
Implement features in small, manageable steps with cleanly cleared context
Validate work as the human in the loop using review, tests, and sub-agent deep reviews
Decide when to handle a change during replanning versus scheduling it as a new roadmap feature
Keep specs and code in sync to prevent drift and reduce cognitive and AI fatigue
Introduce SDD to brownfield/legacy projects by reverse-engineering specs from existing artifacts

skills.skill: Automating and standardizing the SDD workflow
behaviors: Use agent skills to automate repeatable SDD workflows
Choose between MCP servers and CLI-plus-skills for extending an agent
Apply agent standards such as AGENTS.md, Agent Skills, and ACP to stay agent-independent

beginning: Recognize how spec-driven development differs from vibe coding and why specs reduce technical debt.
Identify the core building blocks of the workflow: the constitution's mission, tech stack, and roadmap.
Understand the developer's role as an architect who guides a coding agent rather than writing every line.
developing: Draft a project constitution and feature specs through human-in-the-loop conversation with an agent.
Run the feature loop-plan, implement, and validate-in small, reviewable steps that keep context clean.
Apply spec-driven development to an existing legacy project while keeping specs and code in sync.
accomplished: Decide when to replan versus schedule new roadmap features, managing context and AI fatigue across a project.
Automate repeatable parts of the workflow with agent skills and choose between MCP and CLI-plus-skills.
Leverage agent standards to keep a spec-driven workflow portable across different agents and IDEs.

challenges.scenario: In your first week, a teammate is skeptical that changing how you prompt the agent even matters. To make the case, you need to be clear on what separates quick, prompt-and-hope coding from a disciplined spec-driven approach - and why it matters as the product grows.

questions.behavior: Identify the characteristics and limitations of vibe coding
questions.prompt: You're explaining to your teammate how two ways of working with a coding agent differ. Sort each practice into the approach it best describes.

Vibe coding: Prompting the agent to make it work, eyeballing the result, and re-prompting until it looks right
Relying on a long back-and-forth chat whose history is never saved as a durable artifact
Accepting whatever architectural choices the agent improvises so you can move fast
Spec-driven development: Writing down the problem, success criteria, and constraints before the agent generates code
Keeping a maintained document that persists intent across sessions and even across different agents
Steering large code changes by editing a few sentences of a shared written contract

questions.behavior: Explain the core benefits of specs
questions.prompt: Your teammate asks why writing specs is worth the effort. Group these as a benefit or not a benefit of spec-driven development with a coding agent.

Benefit: Large code changes can be steered by small edits to the spec, cutting cognitive overhead
Essential context persists across sessions, keeping a stateless agent anchored as its window fills
Stating the problem and success criteria up front makes the agent's output match your intent
Not a benefit: A detailed enough spec guarantees correct code, so human review is no longer needed
Specs let the agent run fully autonomously, removing the need for any human decisions

questions.prompt: Your team keeps saying spec-driven development needs a coding agent, not just a chatbot. What capability most distinguishes a coding agent from a chatbot?

options.label: It can read your codebase and use your tools, then plan and act toward a goal
It produces longer, more detailed answers whenever you provide a longer prompt
It automatically refactors your entire codebase
It retains the full chat history so context carries over between sessions

challenges.scenario: With the team on board, you sketch how the work will actually flow - from setting project-wide direction to shipping individual features - and where you, the human, fit into a loop run largely by the agent.

questions.behavior: Describe the cycle of constitution, feature loops, and replanning
questions.prompt: Match each stage of the spec-driven workflow to what it accomplishes.

pairs.right: Sets the project-wide mission, tech stack, and roadmap that guide all future work
Takes one feature through planning, implementation, and validation on its own branch
Revisits the constitution, roadmap, and process between features to adjust course
Reviews and accepts the agent's output, asking for changes where needed

questions.behavior: Recognize the human's role as architect and supervisor who supplies context
questions.prompt: In spec-driven development you act as the architect while the agent does the building. Match each part of your role to what it involves.

pairs.right: Set the goals, constraints, and success criteria in the spec
Follow the agent's progress and steer it when it drifts
Accept the finished work or ask for changes
Leave low-level choices like variable names to the agent

questions.behavior: Select the right level of detail to give an agent
questions.prompt: You're deciding how much detail to put in a spec for the agent. Sort each item by whether it belongs in the spec or is better left to the agent to decide.

Belongs in the spec: The product's mission, target audience, and business constraints
The success criteria and how the feature will be validated
A required technology the whole team must standardize on
Better left to the agent: How a given helper function is implemented internally
Whether to use a `for` loop or a `while` loop

challenges.scenario: It's time to write ContextCafe's constitution: the high-level agreement that will steer every future change. You sit down with the agent to draft it together.

questions.behavior: Identify the three constitution pillars: mission, tech stack, and roadmap
questions.prompt: ContextCafe's constitution has three pillars. Match each pillar to the content it captures.

pairs.right: The project's why: vision, audiences, and scope
Agreed tools, frameworks, and infrastructure for development and deployment
A living sequence of phases, each built as its own feature

questions.behavior: Draft the constitution through human-in-the-loop conversation with the agent
questions.prompt: Working with the agent to draft the constitution, put these collaborative steps in the order the course follows.
correct_order: Give the agent the project description and point it at the stakeholders' notes in the README
Answer the agent's questions about the mission's tone, the tech stack, and roadmap detail
Let the agent turn your answers into the mission, tech-stack, and roadmap files
Review what the agent produced and keep the conversation going to fill any gaps
Commit the constitution so it becomes the project's living reference

questions.behavior: Maintain the constitution as a living, version-controlled document
questions.prompt: You notice the mission left out ContextCafe's target audience. To keep the constitution's related documents complete, what's the best way to fix it according to spec-driven best practice?

options.label: Ask the agent to revise the mission statement
Note the missing audience in the commit message
Ask the agent to add the note only to the code
Keep the audience in a separate file of your own

challenges.scenario: The constitution is committed. Now you tackle the first roadmap feature, moving it through planning, implementation, and validation while keeping each step small enough to review.

questions.behavior: Plan a feature spec covering plan, requirements, and validation before coding
questions.prompt: A feature spec for ContextCafe is organized into three documents. Sort each detail into the document where it belongs.

Plan: The order in which the parts of the feature get built
How the work will be broken into small, reviewable steps
Requirements: The specific API endpoints the feature must expose
The sections the landing page must display
Validation: An automated test asserting the endpoint returns the expected response
The scorecard the agent uses to confirm it met the spec

questions.behavior: Implement features in small, manageable steps with cleanly cleared context
questions.prompt: Put the steps of implementing a spec-driven feature in the order the course follows.
correct_order: Clear the agent's context so it starts from the committed spec rather than stale memory
Prompt the agent to build the task groups defined in the feature plan
Watch the console output to follow the changes the agent makes as it works
Review the diff and, if it's wrong, ask the agent to fix it
Run the app to confirm the corrected feature works

questions.behavior: Validate work as the human in the loop using review, tests, and sub-agent deep reviews
questions.prompt: After the agent implements a feature, you validate it as the human in the loop. Which practices fit that validation step? Select all that apply.

options.label: Reviewing the diff to confirm the feature works and matches the spec
Running the app and stepping through tests under the debugger to confirm behavior
Asking the agent to spawn sub-agents for a deeper review that preserves the main context window
Approving the change because the agent reported that all its tests passed
Focusing the review mainly on code style and naming rather than functional correctness

challenges.scenario: ContextCafe is evolving. Priorities shift, new requirements arrive, and the team even wants to bring an older, spec-less project into the same workflow. You decide how and when to adjust course.

questions.behavior: Decide when to handle a change during replanning versus scheduling it as a new roadmap feature
questions.prompt: During replanning, the product manager asks for a large new capability that will take significant work. How should you handle it?

options.label: Schedule it on the roadmap as its own feature phase, not inline
Start building it right away in the current branch to keep momentum
Prototype it now during replanning and decide later whether to integrate it
Defer it to the next planning cycle without adding it to the roadmap

questions.behavior: Keep specs and code in sync to prevent drift and reduce cognitive and AI fatigue
questions.prompt: Some working habits keep a spec-driven project's specs and code aligned; others let them drift apart. Sort each habit into the right group.

Keeps specs and code aligned: Ask the agent to update related docs whenever the code changes
Work in small steps with frequent commits you can review
Record decisions in the spec, not just in the code
Lets them drift apart: Move files without telling the agent
Hand-edit the code and skip updating the specs
Let the README and specs lag behind the shipped code

questions.behavior: Introduce SDD to brownfield/legacy projects by reverse-engineering specs from existing artifacts
questions.prompt: Put the steps for introducing spec-driven development to an existing, spec-less project in the order the course follows.
correct_order: Point the agent at the existing codebase so it can reverse-engineer a constitution
Commit the reconstructed mission, tech stack, and roadmap as the foundation
Select the highest-priority feature to work on
Plan that feature's specification together with the agent
Build and validate the feature as the human in the loop

challenges.scenario: As the practice spreads across the team, you look for ways to make the workflow faster, repeatable, and portable - so it isn't tied to any one agent or tool.

questions.behavior: Use agent skills to automate repeatable SDD workflows
questions.prompt: Agent skills are best for definable, repeatable workflows. Sort each task by whether it's a good candidate to package as a skill.

Good candidate for a skill: The multi-step prompt you repeat to start every feature spec
Updating the changelog on each merge to main
A validation routine: update the README, lint, format, and write tests
Not a good fit for a skill: Deciding the product's overall mission and target audience
Making a one-time architecture choice unique to this project
Judging whether a risky new feature is worth building at all

questions.behavior: Choose between MCP servers and CLI-plus-skills for extending an agent
questions.prompt: Your team needs to give the agent up-to-date package documentation. You can add it through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, or through a CLI tool invoked by a skill. Why are teams increasingly favoring the CLI-plus-skill option?

options.label: It can take action with less setup than running a dedicated MCP server
It renders documentation with richer formatting than an MCP server provides
It speeds up repeated lookups by keeping a local copy
It queries several package registries at once for broader coverage

questions.behavior: Apply agent standards such as AGENTS.md, Agent Skills, and ACP to stay agent-independent
questions.prompt: Match each agent tool or standard to the role it plays in keeping your workflow from being tied to one agent.

pairs.right: Connects an agent to external tools and data sources
Records project rules and context for the agent
Packages repeatable workflows with the context needed to run them
Bundle installable agent extensions to share across a team
